title: 食料品の消費税がゼロに？

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: Welcome to Japanese Daily News. Today is May twenty-sixth, twenty twenty-six. Today's story: the Japanese government is planning to cut the sales tax on food to zero. Let's listen.

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: 日本政府は、食料品の消費税をゼロパーセントにする方針を発表しました。

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: 今、日本の消費税は10パーセントです。食料品は8パーセントの軽減税率が適用されています。これをゼロにする計画です。

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: 高市早苗首相は、「物価が高くなって、国民の生活が苦しくなっている。食べ物の税金をなくすことで、家計を助けたい」と話しました。

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: この減税は二年間の期間限定です。まず、国会で法案を提出して、早ければ二千二十六年度中に始まる予定です。

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: 例えば、今まで百八円だったおにぎりが、百円になります。千八十円だった食料品の買い物が、千円になります。

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: ただし、お酒と外食は対象外です。スーパーやコンビニで買う食べ物と飲み物だけが対象になります。

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: 野党からは、「ゼロではなく、すべての消費税を下げるべきだ」という意見も出ています。

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: All right. Let's break this down.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: The opening line:

segments.speaker: slow
segments.text: 日本政府は、食料品の消費税をゼロパーセントにする方針を発表しました。

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: The Japanese government announced a plan to make the sales tax on food zero percent. The key words: shokuryouhin means food products or groceries. Shouhizei is consumption tax, or sales tax. And houshin means policy or plan.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: Then we get context about the current tax rate:

segments.speaker: slow
segments.text: 食料品は8パーセントの軽減税率が適用されています。

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: Food currently has a reduced tax rate of eight percent. Keigen zeiritsu means reduced tax rate. Tekiyou sareteimasu means 'is being applied.' Right now Japan has a ten percent sales tax on most things, but food is already lower at eight percent. This plan would take it all the way to zero.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: Prime Minister Takaichi explained why:

segments.speaker: slow
segments.text: 物価が高くなって、国民の生活が苦しくなっている。

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: Prices have risen and people's lives have become difficult. Bukka means prices, as in the general price level. Kurushiku natteiru means 'has become tough.' This is a very natural way to describe financial hardship in Japanese.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: The news gives a concrete example:

segments.speaker: slow
segments.text: 今まで百八円だったおにぎりが、百円になります。

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: An onigiri that used to cost one hundred and eight yen will become one hundred yen. Ima made means 'until now.' Simple math, but it makes the policy feel real.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: And an important exception:

segments.speaker: slow
segments.text: ただし、お酒と外食は対象外です。

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: However, alcohol and eating out are excluded. Tadashi means 'however,' and taishou gai means 'outside the scope' or 'excluded.' So if you buy food at a supermarket or convenience store, no tax. But restaurants and bars, still taxed.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: Today's vocabulary. Shokuryouhin, food products. Shouhizei, consumption tax. Keigen zeiritsu, reduced tax rate. Bukka, price level. Kurushii, tough or difficult. Tadashi, however. Taishou gai, excluded.

segments.speaker: host
segments.text: That's today's Japanese Daily News. Transcript with furigana at jpnotes.dev. See you tomorrow.

segments.speaker: news
segments.text: また明日。
